# Repositioning a 70-Year-Old Brand

*Prove before you proclaim · extend the range, don't replace the meaning · the base forgives, the internet archives*

---

## 1. Unbundle the Problem

"Under-35s think we're outdated" is at least four different problems with different fixes. Most repositionings fail because they treat all four as a meaning problem and solve them with a campaign.

| | **A. Absence** | **B. Meaning** | **C. Offer fit** | **D. Category** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Diagnosis** | They never encounter you where they shop or scroll | They encounter you and read "not for me" | They'd buy the idea but not this format, size, price or ritual | Under-35s consume less of the category at all |
| **Evidence** | Low unprompted awareness, low "seen in last 3 months," low distribution in their channel set | High awareness, low consideration, "my parents' brand" | High consideration, low conversion; trial without repeat | Category penetration falling across all brands |
| **Fix** | Physical + mental availability | Repositioning | Range architecture, pack, price ladder | Occasion extension; brand work won't save you |
| **Cost** | Medium | High and slow | Medium | Very high |

**Most brands assume B. It is usually A and C.** A brand can hold 95% ACV in grocery and be effectively invisible in convenience, quick-commerce, marketplaces, gyms, campuses and social commerce — the places a 27-year-old actually transacts. Measure distribution *in the under-35 channel set* as a separate number before you accept a relevance diagnosis.

---

## 2. Three Diagnostics That Change the Whole Plan

**(a) Age effect or cohort effect?** People join many categories at household formation, not at 24. Compare today's 35–44 penetration to the 35–44 penetration of ten years ago. If today's cohort has caught up on the historical schedule, you are a late-recruitment brand and the panic is misplaced. **If they have not caught up, the cohort is genuinely lost and your franchise will erode exactly as fast as your base ages.** This single comparison sets the urgency, the budget and the tolerance for risk. Run it first.

**(b) Penetration or frequency?** Brand decline is almost always a buyer-count problem, not a loyalty problem. If under-35 decline is penetration, the implication is broad reach, distinctive assets and availability — *not* a narrow, targeted, youth-coded repositioning. Precision targeting is the wrong instrument for a penetration problem.

**(c) How long do you have?** Model profit concentration by age band and decay the base forward. If 60%+ of profit sits with over-55s decaying over a decade, you have roughly three to four years of comfortable investment and then you don't. Put that number on a slide. It ends most internal arguments about pace.

---

## 3. Read the Last Failure Correctly

Two facts in the brief are being misinterpreted internally.

**"It briefly alienated the loyal base."** *Briefly.* The base recovered. That is evidence they are **more robust than the internal risk narrative claims** — and the narrative is now being used to block anything at all. Loyal customers largely do not watch advertising aimed at other people. What actually moves them is a change to the thing they buy: recipe, pack, price, availability, or being made the punchline. Everything else, they tolerate.

**"It was mocked as inauthentic."** This is the durable damage, and it landed on the audience you were trying to win. The base forgives and forgets; the internet archives and re-posts. So the binding constraint on speed is **not** base fragility — it is that under-35s now have a mockery memory of you, and a second attempt at proclamation will be pattern-matched to the first within hours.

**Therefore the sequencing is forced: a period of visible behaviour with no claims attached, long enough to build a record, before any repositioning is said out loud.** You have to earn the right to speak. That is not caution; it is the only route left.

### The five rules of authenticity failure

1. **Borrowed codes.** Slang, memes, aesthetics, music and formats you don't own. Detection is instant and the verdict is *costume*.
2. **Disowning your own customer.** "Not your dad's X" insults the person who is literally your dad, and signals to young people that you are embarrassed of yourself. Embarrassment is unattractive.
3. **Claim without proof.** "Bold. Rebellious. Reinvented." attached to an unchanged product and an unchanged company.
4. **Declaring relevance.** Relevance is conferred by others. A brand that announces it is relevant has demonstrated the opposite.
5. **Speed mismatch.** A nine-month campaign cycle arrives in culture late by construction, wearing last season's reference.

---

## 4. The Positioning Architecture

Separate three layers. Most failed repositionings change the wrong one.

| Layer | Rule | Change frequency |
|---|---|---|
| **Core truth** — why the brand exists and what it has always been good at | **Never replaced. Reframed.** This is what the base owns | Once a generation |
| **Cultural expression** — codes, tone, casting, craft, media, collaborators | Must refresh continuously or it dates | Continuous |
| **Offer** — formats, occasions, price ladder, channels, service | Must be re-fit to how under-35s actually live | Every 2–3 years |

The under-35 problem is almost entirely layers 2 and 3. The instinct to fix it at layer 1 is what alienates the base and produces the costume effect.

### The design test

> **A repositioning is correct when the base reads it as reassurance and the newcomer reads it as discovery — from the same words.**

If the base needs to be persuaded of the new idea, you've changed the core truth. If the newcomer needs the heritage explained apologetically, you've made heritage the theme rather than the proof.

### Recode heritage: proof, not nostalgia

Heritage is not the liability. **Nostalgia posture is** — it excludes everyone who wasn't there. Seventy years is a set of receipts nobody entering the category can buy:

| Nostalgia posture (retire) | Proof posture (adopt) |
|---|---|
| "Remember when…" | "We've had to change this recipe zero times." |
| Sepia, founders' portraits, script type as theme | Archive as raw material, released and remixable |
| "A tradition of quality" | Named standards, published specs, open factory |
| Talking to people who were there | Talking to people who weren't, about what survived |

### Three candidate territories, with fit conditions

Pick on evidence, not taste. All three keep the base whole.

| Territory | Core claim | Fits if | Under-35 tension it resolves |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Permanence as counterculture** | The one thing that hasn't been reformulated, shrunk, hyped or discontinued | Product genuinely unchanged; category is churn-heavy and hype-driven | Exhaustion with disposable, algorithmically-marketed, here-today brands; distrust of new entrants |
| **The standard** | Everyone else is measured against this; we set the bar and never left it | You are the category reference point; competitors imitate your codes | Wanting to buy right the first time; anti-FOMO; competence over novelty |
| **Radical transparency** | Seventy years of the same supply chain, and here it all is | Real, defensible provenance/labour/ingredient story | Verification culture; scepticism of unproven claims |
